chart.x_label: Hour of the day (Pacific), mean over the hours of 2025

series.name: Curtailed, what net load alone predicts

rows.measure: charging, net load and its square held fixed
charging, net load, hour of day and month held fixed

effect_table.in_words: each MW of charging in an hour goes with 0.092 MW less curtailment in that hour, net load, the hour of the day and the month held fixed (standard error 0.011, clustered by day, p < 0.001): an association, not a measured cause, since charging is chosen in the cheap hours, which are the curtailed ones

rows.measure: hours in the sample's top 1 percent

effect_table.in_words: With load, Henry Hub and the month of the year held fixed, each added GW of batteries goes with a multiple 10.76 lower (standard error 2.32, p < 0.001). That is an association in a before-and-after with controls, not a cause: the same years brought the 2021 winter storm, a new offer cap, more solar and a gas price that doubled and fell back.

chart.x_label: day; the 14 days from 7 February 2021 are marked

series.name: control: NYISO New York City real-time price

rows.measure: After the date: the difference in differences (b)
Constant: series minus control before the date (a)
Before the date only: the gap's slope per day over 42 days

effect_table.in_words: In the 14 days from 7 February 2021, ERCOT North Hub real-time price averaged USD 3,047.37 per MWh against USD 21.46 per MWh in the 14 days before, a rise of USD 3,025.91 per MWh. The control, NYISO New York City real-time price, went from USD 56.85 per MWh to USD 66.35 per MWh, a rise of USD 9.51 per MWh. The difference between the two changes is USD 3,016.40 per MWh, standard error USD 1,598.93 per MWh (Newey-West, 3 lags, 28 days). That difference is within 1.96 standard errors of zero: no difference beyond the error. This is the difference between two changes over these days and its error; it does not say what produced it.
